blocks.markdown:
Today's big question: how did people in the past shape our world?

We will meet scholars, a traveller and the founders of Pakistan.
blocks.say: Welcome, history detective! Our big question: how did people from the past shape the world we live in today? We will meet great thinkers of the Golden Age, follow a traveller across half the world, look at ideas that changed life, and discover how our own country began. This is a game, not a test. Let's go!

blocks.alt: People from the past shaped the world we live in.
blocks.caption: People from the past shaped the world we live in.

terms.meaning: A person who studies the past.

blocks.text: Stop 1: A golden age of learning

blocks.markdown:
From about 750 to 1250, scholars in the Muslim world made great discoveries. This time is called the **Golden Age**.

Many worked in the **House of Wisdom** in Baghdad.
blocks.say: From about the year 750 to 1250, scholars in the Muslim world made great discoveries in mathematics, medicine, astronomy and engineering. This time is often called the Golden Age. A famous centre of learning was the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, where scholars gathered books from many lands, translated them, and added new ideas of their own. Let us meet four of these remarkable people.

scenes.caption: Al-Khwarizmi gave us algebra and the word algorithm.
scenes.say: Al-Khwarizmi lived in Baghdad about 1,200 years ago. He wrote a famous book about solving problems with numbers. We get the word algebra from its title. And our word algorithm comes from his name!

scenes.caption: Ibn al-Haytham studied light.
scenes.say: Ibn al-Haytham studied light. He showed that we see because light bounces off objects into our eyes. He tested his ideas with careful experiments, which is why he is called a pioneer of the scientific method.

scenes.caption: Al-Zahrawi was a great surgeon.
scenes.say: Al-Zahrawi was a famous surgeon in Córdoba, in Spain. He wrote a huge medical book, and drew pictures of surgical tools he used, many of them his own inventions.

scenes.caption: Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin.
scenes.say: And Fatima al-Fihri, a woman from a family who moved to Fez, in Morocco, used her inheritance to found a place of learning, the al-Qarawiyyin, in the year 859. It is often called the oldest university still working today.

question.prompt: Which scholar's name gave us the word algorithm?
question.explanation: The word algorithm comes from Al-Khwarizmi's name.

blocks.markdown:
Their ideas are still used today. Many students study **algebra** and science in the same way.

Good scientists test their ideas with **experiments**.
blocks.say: Why do we still remember these people? Because their ideas are still used. Algebra is taught in schools around the world. Ibn al-Haytham's experiments are a model for how scientists work today. Surgeons still use tools like those Al-Zahrawi drew. And Fatima al-Fihri shows that a person with a vision can build something that lasts over a thousand years.

blocks.alt: Algebra, the study of light, surgery and universities all grew from Golden Age scholars.
blocks.caption: Algebra, the study of light, surgery and universities all grew from Golden Age scholars.

question.prompt: Fatima al-Fihri founded a university in Fez, Morocco.

points: The Golden Age ran from about 750 to 1250
Al-Khwarizmi gave us algebra, and Ibn al-Haytham studied light and tested ideas
Al-Zahrawi was a surgeon, and Fatima al-Fihri founded a university
blocks.say: Let us remember. The Golden Age gave us algebra, the study of light, surgery tools and a famous university.

blocks.markdown:
**Ibn Battuta** was born in Morocco in 1304 and travelled for about 30 years.

He covered over 100,000 kilometres and visited the area of today's Pakistan.
blocks.say: Ibn Battuta was born in 1304 in Tangier, in Morocco. When he was twenty-one, he set off to make the pilgrimage to Makkah. But he did not stop there! He kept on travelling for about thirty years, through Egypt, Arabia, Persia, East Africa, India and beyond. He travelled over a hundred thousand kilometres, a distance few people had ever covered. On his way he crossed the area that is today Pakistan, including Sindh and Multan.

scenes.caption: The journey starts in Morocco.
scenes.say: The journey begins in Tangier, in Morocco, in the far west. Ibn Battuta is twenty-one and sets out for Makkah.

scenes.caption: Makkah.
scenes.say: He reaches Makkah and completes the pilgrimage. But he is only just beginning!

scenes.caption: Sindh, Multan and Delhi.
scenes.say: He travels on, across Persia and Central Asia, and arrives in Sindh and Multan, on the Indus, in what is now Pakistan. Then on to Delhi.

scenes.caption: He writes the Rihla.
scenes.say: In the end, he returns home to Morocco and tells his story in a famous book called the Rihla, which means journey.

question.explanation: Ibn Battuta was born in Morocco.

blocks.markdown:
The **Rihla** describes the places and people he met.

Historians use it as a **source** about the past.
blocks.say: Why is his book so valuable? Because he wrote about what he saw: the cities, the markets, the food, and the people he met. Today, historians use the Rihla as a source to learn what life was like in many places about seven hundred years ago. Travellers then needed courage: there were no planes or maps like ours, and the journeys could be dangerous.

blocks.alt: The Rihla tells us what the world was like about 700 years ago.
blocks.caption: The Rihla tells us what the world was like about 700 years ago.

blocks.markdown:
**Paper** made books cheaper. **Algebra** helps solve problems.

Al-Jazari built clever machines, including water clocks.
blocks.say: Many things we use every day grew from old ideas. Paper became common in the Muslim world about twelve hundred years ago, which made books cheaper to make and share. Algebra helps us solve problems in science, building and computers. Hospitals, called bimaristans, cared for sick people and trained doctors. And Al-Jazari, an engineer who lived about 900 years ago, built clever machines, including water clocks and a hand-washing machine that worked a bit like a modern tap.

scenes.caption: Paper.
scenes.say: Paper. Before paper, books were copied by hand onto expensive materials. With paper, many more people could read and learn.

scenes.caption: Algebra.
scenes.say: Algebra. Letters stand for numbers we do not know yet, so we can solve a problem step by step.

scenes.caption: Hospitals.
scenes.say: Hospitals. Doctors treated patients and taught students, and recorded what they learnt.

scenes.caption: Al-Jazari's water clock.
scenes.say: And Al-Jazari's machines. His water clock used the flow of water to tell the time.

blocks.markdown:
Until 1947, the land of Pakistan was part of British India.

Allama Iqbal shared the idea in 1930. The **Lahore Resolution** was passed in 1940.
blocks.say: Now let us come home to our own country. Until 1947, the land we call Pakistan was part of British India. Many Muslims wanted a homeland where they could live their way of life freely. In 1930, the poet and thinker Allama Muhammad Iqbal shared the idea of a Muslim homeland in the north-west. In 1940, on the twenty-third of March, a resolution was passed in Lahore asking for it. The leader of this movement was Muhammad Ali Jinnah, whom we call Quaid-e-Azam.

scenes.caption: 1930: Iqbal's idea.
scenes.say: In 1930, Allama Muhammad Iqbal, a poet and thinker, shared the idea of a homeland for Muslims.

scenes.caption: 1940: The Lahore Resolution.
scenes.say: In 1940, on 23 March, a resolution was passed in Lahore. It is called the Lahore Resolution, and it set out the goal of a homeland.

scenes.caption: 1947: Pakistan is born.
scenes.say: And on 14 August 1947, Pakistan became a new, independent country, with Muhammad Ali Jinnah as its first Governor-General.

question.prompt: On what date did Pakistan become an independent country?

blocks.markdown:
**Quaid-e-Azam** Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the founder of Pakistan.

Allama Iqbal is the national poet. We remember the courage of the families who moved.
blocks.say: Many people helped create Pakistan. Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the founder and first Governor-General. Allama Iqbal is our national poet. Liaquat Ali Khan became the first Prime Minister. Karachi was the first capital, and later Islamabad was built as the new capital. It was also a hard time, because many families had to leave their homes and move to a new place, and we remember their courage and hope.

blocks.alt: Pakistan's flag has a crescent and a star. We celebrate Independence Day on 14 August.
blocks.caption: Pakistan's flag has a crescent and a star. We celebrate Independence Day on 14 August.
